questions.question: Why do closures in loops capture wrong values, and how do you fix it?
questions.title: Closures Loop Capture
questions.direct_answer: A closure captures the VARIABLE, not its current value. In a `var` loop, all closures share ONE binding — they all see the final value after the loop ends. Fixes: let (a fresh binding per iteration — the modern answer), an IIFE (creates a new scope per iteration — the pre-let answer), or bind the value as a parameter. The bug class: any callback created in a loop and deferred (timers, event handlers, promises) reads stale shared state.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    V[var loop: ONE binding] --> C1[closure 1] & C2[closure 2] & C3[closure 3]
    C1 & C2 & C3 -->|all read the SAME slot at fire time| F[3, 3, 3]
    L[let loop: fresh binding PER iteration] --> K1[closure 1 own i=0] & K2[closure 2 own i=1] & K3[closure 3 own i=2]
    K1 & K2 & K3 --> R[0, 1, 2]
    IIFE[IIFE: parameter copy per call] --> R
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The spec mechanics (what 'per-iteration binding' means): each iteration of a let-loop is semantically a new lexical environment — CreatePerIterationEnvironment copies the loop variables' CURRENT values into fresh bindings at each iteration start (that's why modifications inside the closure of iteration 2 don't affect iteration 3's view, and why the next iteration still sees the updated counter — the copy happens at the right points). var has no such machinery: one function-scoped binding, one shared capture.

The general capture semantics (beyond loops): closures capture the binding — so reassignment AFTER capture is VISIBLE to the closure (counters work: let count = 0; const inc = () => ++count). Two closures over the same binding SHARE state (inc and read both see count). A closure over a const captures an immutable binding to a (possibly mutable) object. The full model: capture = reference to the environment record; value lookups happen at CALL time — which is why stale-value bugs are really stale-BINDING bugs.

The memory dimension (the production close): a closure keeps its captured environment alive as long as the closure lives — an event handler capturing a large object leaks that object until the handler is removed. The classic leak: long-lived listener capturing per-request state. The discipline: remove listeners when done (AbortController for addEventListener!), capture the minimum (destructure just the id, not the whole item), and know that closures are the MECHANISM behind module pattern, memoization caches, and every hook — this question is the same knowledge as 'why does a hook remember state between renders.'
